newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin official warns against regional separatism.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin official warns against regional separatism.

text.p: A senior presidential aide warned on Monday that a string of gubernatorial elections this autumn would dangerously weaken Moscow's control over the 89 regions which form the vast Russian federation.
First deputy head of the presidential administration Alexander Kazakov told a news conference that the Kremlin was preparing measures to rein in influential regional leaders.

"We have a paradoxical situation here in Russia," Kazakov said. "When the (electoral) campaign ends we will have leaders who will not be controlled by president, government, local legislature or anyone at all."
Kazakov said that this threat was far more important than the actual results of the polls, which are being held over several months starting in late August.
He said that out of 14 regional elections held so far, the Kremlin's candidates had clearly lost in three places -- central Kursk and Kirov regions and Pskov in the west.

The Russian constitution adopted in December 1993 provided for direct elections of regional governors and most other top provincial officials, bringing them into line with the directly elected heads of Russia's ethnic republics.
But until recently most governors, under transitional constitutional arrangements, were appointed and sacked by President Boris Yeltsin rather than popularly elected.
The current series of gubernatorial elections will put an end to this situation, vastly reducing the Kremlin's powers of patronage over the regions.
"I try hard to find a single positive element in the very idea of these elections and I can't," said Kazakov.

Yeltsin, who in October 1993 crushed a bloody revolt in Moscow by supporters of the Soviet-era legislature, made sure that the new constitution adopted later that year limited the powers of parliament.
The Kremlin has implicitly encouraged appointed regional governors to grab more powers at the expense of regional councils or assemblies, most of which backed Yeltsin's opponents in 1993.

"They (gubernatorial hopefuls) look forward to taking part in elections to become more independent from the centre," Kazakov added. "No doubt, separatism will rise after the polls. There should not be any illusions about this."

Apart from rebel Chechnya, no other Russian regions have seriously tried to secede from the federation. But most have tried to claw back as much authority as possible from Moscow and contribute as little as possible to the federal budget.

Regional leaders reacted angrily last week when Yeltsin's chief of staff Anatoly Chubais, increasingly powerful in the absence of the ailing president, called for a reassertion of the authority of central government over the regions.

Chubais, who has launched a crusade to stop widespread tax dodging, threatened several big regional firms with bankruptcy and told regional leaders to change their legislation to conform with federal law.

Last week Justice Minister Valentin Kovalyov told a news conference that the constitutions of 19 out of Russia's 21 ethnic republics contradicted the federal constitution, as did a mass of regional legislation.
The leader of the powerful ethnic republic of Tatarstan, Mintimer Shaimiyev, told the Kremlin flatly that nothing would take place in his region without his approval.
His opposition forced the Kremlin to back down on its threat to declare the giant KamAZ truck factory in Tatarstan bankrupt.
The president of the ethnic republic of North Ossetia, Akhsarbek Galazov, generally known for his pro-Moscow views, warned that further pressure on the regions could lead to crisis.
"Any humiliation of regional power will help Russia's enemies," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying. "Then a threat of separatism could emerge."
Kazakov said the presidential administration was preparing a draft law which would reduce the independence of regional leaders.
But he did not say how such a draft could pass the Federation Council upper house of parliament where regional leaders occupy half of the seats and heads of regional councils the other half.
